source.notes: Official CISCE item bank 'ISC Competency Focused Practice Questions, Artificial Intelligence, Class - XI' (cover prints 'cLASS - XI'; page headers 'ISC-Class XI'; 'First edition: August 2026'; preface by the Chief Executive & Secretary dated 31st August 2026; file uploaded to cisce.org in 2026/09). It is a question bank, not an examination paper: examYear is null and no maximum marks or duration are printed. 31 PDF pages: questions on printed pages 1-18 (PDF pages 6-23; PDF page = printed page + 5), Answer Key on printed pages 19-25 (PDF pages 24-30). 76 questions in five sections with marks in each section header: I MCQs (Q1-25, 1 mark each), II Assertion-Reason (Q26-31, 1 mark each), III Very Short Answer (Q32-56, 1 mark each), IV Short Answer (Q57-71, 2 marks each), V Long Answer (Q72-76, 10 marks each); marksSource is SECTION_INSTRUCTIONS and the 136-mark total is just the sum of the bank. Multi-part questions (sub-part marks printed in brackets) are kept as one entry. Each question prints a topic tag in square brackets and a cognitive domain in parentheses (recorded as cognitiveLevel). The document uses a math font whose text layer doubles or garbles italic letters (e.g. 'AA' for A, wrong letters in Q19); those expressions were rebuilt from the rendered pages and flagged MEDIUM. officialAnswer comes from the bank's own Answer Key, which 'presents the possible answers to a given question, but it is neither limiting nor exhaustive'; copied as printed, never extended. Code in the answer key is kept line by line; its display indentation (proportional font) is approximated. The copyright page reserves all rights; reproduction here is for study with attribution and a link to the original.

questions.text: Which one of the following is most likely a probabilistic problem?
options: Calculating simple interest on a fixed deposit
Checking whether a number is even or odd
Predicting tomorrow’s rainfall in a city

questions.text:
A retail company builds a linear regression model to predict daily sales from advertising expenditure. After training, the data scientist notices that the model’s predicted sales are very close to the actual sales, so the residuals (errors) are very small. The company plans to use these predictions for inventory planning and budgeting.
In this situation, why is it important for the model to have small residuals?
options: To reduce randomness in the data
To increase the value of the regression slope
To improve the accuracy of sales predictions
To remove unnecessary data points

officialAnswer.text: (c) To improve the accuracy of sales predictions

questions.text: Why is min‑max scaling often used before distance-based algorithms?
options: It converts all values to integers
It makes all features have the same number of unique values
It brings features to a similar range so one feature does not dominate due to scale

officialAnswer.text: (c) It brings features to a similar range so one feature does not dominate due to scale

Unstructured: no fixed format; example: social media images and posts.

questions.text: State any two strategies to reduce bias in AI systems.

officialAnswer.text: Use diverse/representative data; fairness audits; regular testing; human review; reweighting and balancing data.

questions.text: How can gender imbalance in the training data of a hiring model create biased outcomes?

officialAnswer.text: If historical data contains mostly male hires, the model may learn that “male” patterns are associated with success and may unfairly rank female candidates lower, even when equally qualified.

questions.text: Why is transparency important when AI is used in high‑stakes decisions (e.g., admissions, loans)?

officialAnswer.text: People affected need to know that AI is being used, understand basic reasons for decisions, and have a way to question or appeal, which builds trust and helps detect errors or bias.

questions.text: Explain why children’s data needs extra protection in AI systems used in schools.

officialAnswer.text: Children are more vulnerable, may not fully understand risks, and misuse of their data can harm them for years (profiling, exploitation); hence stronger consent, minimization, and safeguards are required.

questions.text: A dataset of monthly online orders is: 20, 22, 25, 50. Compute the mean and median using Python.
extractionIssues: The bank tags this question [Basic Concepts of Artificial Intelligence]; chapter suggested from the content

officialAnswer.text:

questions.text: Briefly explain what is meant by dimensionality of data. How does high dimensionality impact visualization?

• High dimensionality (many features) makes direct human visualization difficult; we must use projections (e.g., PCA), pairplots, or encode multiple dimensions via color, size, etc.

questions.text:
A hospital collects patient data to predict risk of heart disease. The dataset includes age, blood pressure, cholesterol, and exercise frequency. Issues found:
• Some rows have missing cholesterol values
• Several rows are exact duplicates
• Exercise frequency is stored as "low", "medium", "high" in some rows and 0,1,2 in others
(a) Identify two data quality problems from the above and explain how each can affect the AI model.
(b) Write Python code using Pandas to:
• Drop duplicate rows, and
• Replace missing cholesterol values with the mean cholesterol.
Assume the DataFrame is named df and cholesterol column is "cholesterol".
(c) Name a suitable graph type to visualise the distribution of cholesterol values and explain why it is appropriate.
extractionIssues: Sub-part marks printed (a) [4], (b) [3], (c) [3]; kept as one 10-mark entry

officialAnswer.text:
(a) Any two
• Missing values: leaving them untreated may cause errors in training or biased patterns if many rows are dropped.
• Duplicate rows: over‑represent certain patients, biasing the model towards repeating those patterns.
• Inconsistent formats for the same feature (exercise frequency): model or preprocessing code may misinterpret categories, leading to wrong one‑hot encoding or numerical mapping.
(b) Suggested Python code:
import pandas as pd
# Drop duplicate rows
df = df.drop_duplicates()
# Fill missing cholesterol values with column mean
df['cholesterol'].fillna(df['cholesterol'].mean(), inplace=True)
(c) A histogram: It shows how cholesterol values are distributed across ranges, making it easy to spot skewness and outliers.

questions.text:
An e‑commerce site wants to recommend AI‑related courses. They have:
• Browsing history: courses viewed by each user
• Purchase history: courses bought by each user
• Ratings (1 to 5 stars) for purchased courses
(a) Explain how the concepts of union and intersection can help in designing recommendation logic.
(b) Assume you have a CSV file "courses.csv" with columns: "user_id", "course_name", "rating".
Write Python code to:
• Load it into a DataFrame df, and
• Display the first five rows of only "user_id" and "course_name" columns.
(c) Explain how mean rating and number of ratings for each course can be used together for better recommendations.
extractionIssues: Sub-part marks printed (a) [4], (b) [3], (c) [3]; kept as one 10-mark entry

officialAnswer.text:
(a) For a user, the union of viewed and purchased courses gives the set of all courses they have shown interest in; useful to infer preferences and build profile.
The intersection across users (courses that many people both view and buy) helps identify popular, high‑interest courses to recommend to similar users.
(b) Suggested Python code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('courses.csv')
print(df[['user_id', 'course_name']].head())
(c) Mean rating shows average satisfaction, but a high mean from only a few ratings may not be reliable.
Combining mean rating with count of ratings helps prefer courses that are both well‑liked and widely rated, adding robustness.

questions.text:
A company analyses three AI courses offered to students: AI Basics, Data Science, and Robotics. The data is:
Course | Students | Average Score
AI Basics | 50 | 80
Data Science | 35 | 76
Robotics | 25 | 72
(a) Write Python code using `matplotlib` to plot a bar chart for the number of students in each course.
(b) Suggest one additional graph type to compare average scores across the three courses and justify why it is effective.
(c) Based on the data, mention one insight and one recommendation for the school.
extractionIssues: Sub-part marks printed (a) [4], (b) [3], (c) [3]; kept as one 10-mark entry
Table on page 23 reproduced as text rows (cells separated by '|'); check against the PDF

officialAnswer.text:
(a) Python code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
courses = ['AI Basics', 'Data Science', 'Robotics']
students = [50, 35, 25]
plt.figure(figsize=(6, 4))
plt.bar(courses, students, color=['#4E79A7', '#F28E2B', '#76B7B2'],
edgecolor='black')
plt.title('Number of Students per Course')
plt.xlabel('Course')
plt.ylabel('Number of Students')
plt.show()
(b)
• A bar chart of average scores is effective because it clearly shows the relative performance of each course (height of bars directly comparable).
• Alternatively, a line graph with courses on the x-axis and average scores on the y-axis can show performance trend across courses. Explanation must mention ease of comparison.
(c)
• Insight: AI Basics has the highest enrolment and highest average score; Robotics has lowest enrolment and lowest scores.
• Recommendation: Strengthen Robotics course (resources, teaching strategies) or promote it more to increase interest and performance.
